section: Growth by imbibition versus crystal growth
label: Fluid protoplasm growing by imbibition produces rounded rather than plane surfaces
claim: Because protoplasm is fluid and grows by imbibition (intussusception) rather than by deposition of particles on a surface, freely growing organisms tend to have swelling, rounded contours, and plane surfaces are rare in them unless produced by pressure.
quote: So far then, as growth goes on, unaffected by pressure or other external force, the fluidity of protoplasm, its mobility internal and external, and the manner in which particles move with comparative freedom from place to place within, all manifestly tend to the production of swelling, rounded surfaces, and to their great predominance over plane surfaces in the contour of the organism.
scope: living cells and organisms growing free of external pressure, contrasted with crystals
measurable_quantities: proportion of curved versus planar surface in cell and organism outlines
candidate_data: 3D cell segmentation and shape datasets such as the Allen Cell Explorer and Image Data Resource, compared with crystal morphology databases.

section: Surface tension and the forms of cells
label: Surface tension is probably the paramount force determining cell form
claim: Of the physical forces that determine the forms of cells, solitary or in contact, surface tension is of great and probably paramount importance, usually acting together with gravity, mechanical pressure and osmosis.
quote: Among the forces which determine the forms of cells, whether they be solitary or arranged in contact with one another, this force of surface-tension is certainly of great, and is probably of paramount importance.
scope: all cells, solitary or in aggregates
candidate_data: Published micropipette aspiration and AFM measurements of cortical tension paired with cell shape imaging, e.g. Allen Cell Explorer and Image Data Resource datasets.

label: Organic symmetry reflects equilibrium and is absent without it, as in amoeba
claim: Symmetry is highly characteristic of organic forms because they are figures of equilibrium governed by a principle of minimal energy, as in liquid films; symmetry is lacking only where equilibrium is lacking, as in the amoeba.
quote: Such symmetry is in a high degree characteristic of organic forms, and is rarely absent in living things,—save in such cases as amoeba, where the equilibrium on which symmetry depends is likewise lacking.
scope: organic forms generally, especially cells
candidate_data: Time-lapse cell shape datasets (e.g. Image Data Resource, Cell Image Library) allowing comparison of symmetry measures between motile and resting cells.

section: Surface tension in protoplasm and amoeba
label: Rounding off of protoplasm is due to surface tension, not vital contractility
claim: When a drop of protoplasm, or the tip of an amoeba's pseudopodium, rounds itself off, this is a simple consequence of surface tension and not of any special vital contractility.
quote: When any drop of protoplasm, either over all its surface or at some free end, as at the extremity of the pseudopodium of an amoeba, is seen likewise to “round itself off,” that is not an effect of “vital contractility,” but (as Hofmeister shewed so long ago as 1867) a simple consequence of surface tension
scope: naked protoplasm, amoeboid cells and pseudopodia
measurable_quantities: effect of inhibiting active contractile machinery on rounding
candidate_data: Published cell-rounding and cortical tension measurements with and without myosin inhibition; live-imaging datasets in the Image Data Resource.

section: Surface tension in protoplasm and amoeba
label: Plasmodial taxes towards moisture, warmth and food parallel surface-tension phenomena
claim: The movements of a plasmodium (Aethalium) towards damp, warm or nutritious spots and away from sugar or salt solutions can each be accounted for by local changes of surface tension, as in inanimate drops moving on a warmed or chemically altered surface.
quote: When we find that a plasmodium of Aethalium, for instance, creeps towards a damp spot, or towards a warm spot, or towards substances that happen to be nutritious, and again creeps away from solutions of sugar or of salt, we seem to be dealing with phenomena every one of which can be paralleled by ordinary phenomena of surface tension
scope: slime-mould plasmodia and amoeboid organisms
measurable_quantities: direction and speed of migration in gradients
local surface tension of the plasmodium
candidate_data: Published Physarum chemotaxis and thermotaxis assays and tension/rheology measurements; none known as a central database.

section: Surface tension in protoplasm and amoeba
label: Resting cells are spherical; the amoeboid phase is one of activity and unequal tensions
claim: In naked protoplasmic cells the amoeboid form marks a phase of activity with unequal surface tensions, whereas the spherical form marks a phase of rest when internal homogeneity and minimal potential energy are attained, at which time the cell also becomes encysted.
quote: In the case of the naked protoplasmic cell, as the amoeboid phase is emphatically a phase of freedom and activity, of chemical and physiological change, so, on the other hand, is the spherical form indicative of a phase of rest or comparative inactivity.
scope: naked protoplasmic cells, amoebae and other protists with resting stages
candidate_data: Imaging and encystment studies of Acanthamoeba and other amoebae; Image Data Resource time-lapse datasets.

section: Budding yeast and localised tension changes
label: A yeast bud arises where surface tension locally and suddenly diminishes
claim: A bud appears on a yeast cell because the surface tension diminishes at one part of the cell surface, so that this area expands, after which the bud's own surface tension rounds it into a roughly spherical form.
quote: When a “bud” appears, whether with or without actual growth by osmosis or otherwise of the mass, it does so because at a certain part of the cell-surface the surface tension has more or less suddenly diminished, and the area of that portion expands accordingly
scope: budding yeast cells
measurable_quantities: local cell-wall or membrane tension and extensibility at the bud site
candidate_data: Yeast cell-wall mechanics (AFM) and bud morphology imaging, e.g. SCMD (Saccharomyces cerevisiae Morphological Database).

label: Each new foraminiferal chamber is a surface-tension figure; the whole shell is not
claim: In multichambered organisms such as the foraminifera Globigerina or Rotalia, and in desmids, each newly formed bud or chamber is a figure of equilibrium shaped by surface tension while still fluid, and is then solidified onto earlier chambers, so the whole organism is not itself a figure of minimal area.
quote: The little organism as a whole is not a figure of equilibrium or of minimal area; but each new bud or separate chamber is such a figure, conditioned by the forces of surface tension, and superposed upon the complex aggregate of similar bubbles after these latter have become consolidated one by one into a rigid system.
scope: multichambered foraminifera, desmids and other organisms formed by successive stages of growth and consolidation
measurable_quantities: shape of individual chambers (closeness to constant-mean-curvature surfaces)
candidate_data: Micro-CT foraminiferal shell scans in MorphoSource and published 3D chamber reconstructions; Endless Forams image collection.

label: Surface tension governs the forms of small organisms and cells, not large organisms
claim: Surface tension governs form only where surface energy is a large fraction of total energy, so it determines the forms of minute organisms and of the small cells of larger organisms, while the general forms of large organisms are due to other, non-molecular forces.
quote: in other words it will be small or minute organisms, or the small cellular elements of larger organisms, whose forms will be governed by surface-tension; while the general forms of the larger organisms will be due to other and non-molecular forces.
scope: organisms and cells across sizes
measurable_quantities: agreement of shape with surface-tension figures
candidate_data: Cell and organism size and shape compilations (e.g. Allen Cell Explorer for cells, AnimalTraits for body size) combined with shape measurements.

section: Plateau's surfaces of revolution in cells
label: Spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest unicellular forms
claim: Of the six surfaces of revolution with constant mean curvature (plane, sphere, cylinder, catenoid, unduloid, nodoid), spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest forms of small unicellular organisms and of cells in simple aggregates, and transitions between them are frequent during growth, reproduction and development.
quote: That spheres, cylinders and unduloids are of the commonest occurrence among the forms of small unicellular organism, or of individual cells in the simpler aggregates, and that in the processes of growth, reproduction and development transitions are frequent from one of these forms to another, is obvious to the naturalist
scope: unicellular organisms and cells of simple aggregates
measurable_quantities: fit of cell outlines to sphere, cylinder and unduloid profiles
candidate_data: Protist and bacterial image collections (e.g. EcoTaxa plankton images, Image Data Resource, Cell Image Library) analysed for shape classes.

label: A cylindrical cell's end cap has twice the cylinder's radius and height about 0.27R
claim: Where a cylindrical cell of uniform wall tension is capped by part of a sphere, the sphere's radius is twice the cylinder's radius, the cap subtends a cone of 60°, and its height is about 0.27 of the cylinder radius (a little more than one-eighth of the diameter), proportions seen in the free end cells of Spirogyra.
quote: the normal height of the spherical cap over the end of the cylindrical cell is just a very little more than one-eighth of the diameter of the cylinder, or of the radius of the sphere. And these are the proportions which we recognise, under normal circumstances, in such a case as the cylindrical cell of Spirogyra where its free end is capped by a portion of a sphere.
scope: cylindrical cells with free spherical ends, e.g. Spirogyra and other filamentous algae
candidate_data: Micrographs of filamentous algae and of rod-shaped bacteria pole geometry from published imaging datasets (e.g. Image Data Resource).

section: Instability of liquid cylinders and beading
label: Viscid spider-thread coating breaks into beads at the cylinder stability limit
claim: The sticky fluid coating of a spider's spiral thread, being a liquid cylinder, becomes unstable when its length exceeds its circumference and breaks up into equal, equally spaced beads (often with smaller beads between), the spacing being somewhat greater than theory owing to viscosity and drag on the core thread.
quote: But this liquid cylinder has its limit of stability when its length equals its own circumference, and therefore just at the points so defined it tends to disrupt into separate segments
scope: viscid capture threads of orb-weaving spiders; liquid films on fibres
candidate_data: Published measurements of glue droplet spacing and size on orb-web capture threads (including datasets deposited on Dryad).

label: Notched hydroid cups and annulated stems are both due to surface tension
claim: The notching of the rim of hydroid calycles and the annular constrictions of their cylindrical stems are phenomena of the same order, both produced by surface tension acting on the structures while they are still fluid or semifluid films, as in the beaded rim of a splash.
quote: In the case of the hydroid calycle (Fig. 72), we are led to the conclusion that the two common and conspicuous features of notching or indentation of the cup, and of constriction or annulation of the long cylindrical stem, are phenomena of the same order and are due to surface-tension in both cases alike.
scope: calycles and stems of campanularian hydroids and other small organic cups
measurable_quantities: number and spacing of rim teeth relative to rim circumference
annulation spacing relative to stem diameter
candidate_data: Hydroid specimen images in museum collections and GBIF-linked media, with morphometric measurement.

label: Freely growing cylindrical cells owe their form to an anisotropic wall
claim: A cylindrical cell such as Spirogyra that grows without external restraint takes its form because its developing membrane is anisotropic, extending more easily in one direction; a slight inequality of tension in two directions gives an ellipsoidal cell and a great inequality a cylindrical one.
quote: I take it therefore, that the cylindrical cell of Spirogyra, or any other cylindrical cell which grows in freedom from any manifest external restraint, has assumed that particular form simply by reason of the molecular constitution of its developing surface-membrane; and that this molecular constitution was anisotropous, in such a way as to render extension easier in one direction than another.
scope: elongated plant cells, algae, yeasts and other walled cells grown free of external restraint
candidate_data: Published cellulose microfibril orientation and wall mechanics data for algal and plant cells; Plant Cell Atlas imaging resources.

section: Limited range of forms in small organisms
label: Small organisms show a limited range of forms because molecular forces control them
claim: Because protozoa, bacteria and other minute cells are of a size at which form is mainly controlled by molecular forces, they exhibit only a limited range of forms, which vary with physical conditions.
quote: To the fact that these little organisms belong to an order of magnitude in which form is mainly, if not wholly, conditioned and controlled by molecular forces, is due the limited range of forms which they actually exhibit.
scope: unicellular organisms, bacteria, spores and free cells
measurable_quantities: morphological disparity (shape diversity) versus organism size
candidate_data: Large plankton and microbial image sets (e.g. EcoTaxa) and bacterial shape compilations compared with metazoan morphospace data from Phenoscape or MorphoSource.

section: Limited range of forms in small organisms
label: Bacterial form is too plastic to serve for species identification
claim: Bacteria and micrococci change shape so much with life stage, circumstances and preparation that their specific identity can seldom be recognised by form, so they have a physiological rather than morphological specificity.
quote: Whatever grounds we may have for attributing to these organisms a permanent or stable specific identity (after the fashion of the higher plants and animals), we can seldom safely do so on the ground of definite and always recognisable _form_
scope: bacteria and micrococci
candidate_data: Bacterial cell morphology imaging datasets across growth conditions (e.g. published Dryad and Image Data Resource collections) paired with species identity.

label: Vorticella bells form a graded series of unduloids
claim: The bells of the various species of Vorticella, like many other Infusoria, are unduloids or partial unduloids spanning every gradation from nearly cylindrical to nearly spherical, bounded by the stalk attachment and the ciliary ring as by two unequal supporting rings, and the species differ only in ratio or degree.
quote: The cups of the various species of Vorticella (Fig. 75) are nothing in the world but a beautiful series of unduloids, or partial unduloids, in every gradation from a form that is all but cylindrical to one that is all but a perfect sphere.
scope: Vorticella and other cup-shaped or flask-shaped ciliates and flagellates
measurable_quantities: ratio of neck to bulge radius
candidate_data: Ciliate micrograph collections (e.g. EcoTaxa, published Vorticella morphometric studies) for outline fitting.

label: Protozoan loricas form by adsorption into least-area surfaces, not for protection
claim: The membranous cups (loricas) of Salpingoeca, Tintinnus and similar protozoa arise inevitably from substances adsorbed in the surface layer of the protoplasm, and molecular forces make the resulting pellicle a surface of least possible area under the circumstances, here an unduloid; this efficient cause, rather than a protective purpose, explains their form.
quote: that this surface pellicle or membrane was inevitably bound, by molecular forces, to become a surface of the least possible area which the circumstances permitted
scope: loricate protozoa such as Salpingoeca, Tintinnus, Dinobryon and Codonella
candidate_data: Tintinnid lorica morphometric datasets and plankton imaging collections such as EcoTaxa.

label: Shared form in simple organisms need not imply common descent
claim: The assumption that similar or identical forms indicate genealogical relationship is far less well founded for minute organisms with few, simple characters whose form is largely produced directly by a physical force, so identical forms of such organisms in different times or places need not indicate unbroken descent or common stock.
quote: when we attempt to extend it to minute organisms whose specific characters are few and simple, whose simplicity becomes much more manifest when we regard it from the point of view of physical and mathematical description and analysis, and whose form is referable, or (to say the least of it) is very largely referable, to the direct and immediate action of a particular physical force.
scope: minute organisms such as foraminifera (e.g. Lagena), infusoria and radiolaria
candidate_data: Molecular phylogenies of foraminifera and ciliates (e.g. PR2 ribosomal database, GenBank sequences) compared with morphospecies assignments and fossil occurrences in the Paleobiology Database.

section: Foraminiferal shells and position of symmetry
label: The unduloid Lagena shell is formed while hanging vertically in the sea
claim: The flask-shaped (unduloid) shell of Lagena is formed while the organism hangs vertically, in a position of symmetry about its vertical axis, like a hanging drop; flattened or winged forms are those formed when this symmetry of position was absent and the shell lay horizontally.
quote: but we may be pretty sure that it is suspended vertically in the sea, that is to say in a position of symmetry as regards its vertical axis, about which the unduloid surface of revolution is symmetrically formed.
scope: monothalamous calcareous foraminifera (Lagena) and, by extension, flask-shaped pteropod shells
measurable_quantities: orientation of living organism during shell formation
presence of lateral flattening or wings
candidate_data: Field and culture observations of Lagena life position and shell morphometrics from foraminiferal collections; none known as a database.

label: Thin walls flute longitudinally; thick narrow necks pleat transversely
claim: Small tension changes in a thin-walled elongated cell produce wrinkling in the plane of greatest curvature, hence longitudinal fluting, especially near the ends; where the wall is thick relative to diameter, as in the narrow neck of Lagena or tubular hydroid gonangia, bending stiffness makes folding transverse instead.
quote: The manner in which our little Lagena-shell tends to fold or wrinkle, longitudinally in its wider part, and transversely or annularly in its narrow neck, is thus completely and easily explained.
scope: Lagena and other foraminifera, campanularian gonangia, and similar thin-walled elongated organic vesicles
candidate_data: Foraminiferal shell images and micro-CT in MorphoSource and museum collections, measured for fold orientation and wall thickness.

label: Symmetrical surface-tension pull sets heliozoan filaments radially
claim: Fluid surface protoplasm creeps up the stiff axial filaments of a heliozoan such as Actinophrys, and because this surface-tension pull is symmetrical around each filament the filaments are set normal to the cell surface, radiating from the centre; closely spaced filaments produce honeycomb-like depressions between them.
quote: Since the attraction exercised by this surface tension is symmetrical around the filament, the latter will be pulled equally in all directions; in other words it will tend to be set normally to the surface of the sphere, that is to say radiating directly outwards from the centre.
scope: Heliozoa and radiolarians with radiating axopodia or spicules
measurable_quantities: angle of axopodia to cell surface
contact-angle profile of protoplasm on filaments
candidate_data: Published imaging of heliozoan axopodia; no dedicated database known.

label: The trypanosome undulating membrane is a liquid film drawn up along a flagellum
claim: The undulating membrane of trypanosomes and related flagellates forms when the flagellum lies near and parallel to the body and the fluid surface protoplasm is drawn up as a film along it, as a soap-film would be; the membrane is thus a liquid film of constant mean curvature whose undulations are produced by molecular tensions, not by its own active mobility.
quote: It is a plausible assumption to suppose that, as the flagellum waves about, it comes to lie near and parallel to the body of the cell, and that the frill or undulating membrane is formed by the clear, fluid protoplasm of the surface layer springing up in a film to run up and along the flagellum, just as a soap-film would be formed in similar circumstances.
scope: trypanosomes, Trichomonas and related flagellates, and spermatozoa with undulating membranes
candidate_data: Electron microscopy and live imaging of trypanosome and Trichomonas morphology, e.g. the TrypTag localisation resource and the Image Data Resource.

label: The biconcave red blood corpuscle is not a surface-tension equilibrium figure
claim: The biconcave mammalian red blood corpuscle is not a surface of constant mean curvature and so cannot be a fluid drop in equilibrium under surface tension alone; some other force, possibly osmotic inequilibrium or fluid-crystal forces of its cholesterin-like constituents, must maintain its shape, which changes to a sphere in diluted blood.
quote: Accordingly, from the point of view of surface tension alone, the blood-corpuscle is not a surface of equilibrium; or in other words, it is not a fluid drop suspended in another liquid.
scope: mammalian and other vertebrate red blood cells
candidate_data: Published erythrocyte shape and osmotic fragility datasets and red cell membrane mechanics measurements.

label: Decapod sperm-cell shape is an intermediate phase of osmotic shrinkage
claim: The normal form of decapod crustacean sperm-cells is one of many intermediate phases of shrinkage from a spherical form, caused by osmotic withdrawal of fluid without a matching reduction of surface area, so that equivalent shapes are produced by salt solutions of equivalent (molecular-weight-proportional) concentration.
quote: we see that what we call its normal appearance is just one of many intermediate phases of shrinkage, brought about by the abstraction of fluid from its interior as the result of an osmotic pressure greater outside than inside the cell
scope: sperm-cells of decapod crustacea (Inachus, Galathea, Dromia, crayfish) and, by comparison, red blood cells
measurable_quantities: cell shape as a function of external osmolarity
candidate_data: Published osmotic-response studies of decapod spermatozoa; no dedicated database known.

label: Elastic fibrillae act as a microscopic skeleton shaping spiral cells
claim: The spiral and other peculiar forms of decapod sperm-cells and of many Infusoria are produced by more or less elastic fibrillae in the cell, which restrain and modify the surface forces like the wire frames and coils in Plateau's experiments, acting as a microscopic skeleton.
quote: In all probability we must in like manner attribute the peculiar spiral and other forms, for instance of many Infusoria, to the presence, among the multitudinous other differentiations of their protoplasmic substance, of such more or less elastic fibrillae, which play as it were the part of a microscopic skeleton
scope: Infusoria, decapod sperm-cells and other cells with non-equilibrium shapes
measurable_quantities: presence and arrangement of cortical fibrillar structures
change of shape when fibrils are disrupted
candidate_data: Electron microscopy and cytoskeleton imaging of ciliates and sperm cells, e.g. the Cell Image Library and EMPIAR.

label: Cell-wall secretion is adsorption of constituents at the surface
claim: The so-called secretion of a cell-wall or membrane is the adsorption of certain constituents of the cell, which lower surface tension, to its surface (as formulated by the Gibbs-Thomson law), where they also increase viscosity and rigidity; the formation of a cell membrane is thus a chemico-physical phenomenon.
quote: The so-called “secretion” of this cell-wall is nothing more than a sort of exudation, or striving towards the surface, of certain constituent molecules or particles within the cell; and the Gibbs-Thomson law formulates, in part at least, the conditions under which they do so.
scope: cell-walls and membranes of protozoa, plant cells and blood corpuscles
measurable_quantities: surface concentration of wall materials during wall formation
candidate_data: Biochemical and imaging studies of cell-wall deposition; no single database known.

label: Spicules are deposited at interfaces between cells or vacuoles
claim: Skeletal spicules, as in sponges and radiolaria, are characteristically deposited in the interfacial boundaries between cells or vacuoles, and their form is in many cases regulated by the arrangement of these boundaries.
quote: it is highly characteristic of the whole process of spicule-formation for the deposits to be laid down just in the “interfacial” boundaries between cells or vacuoles, and that the form of the spicular structures tends in many cases to be regulated and determined by the arrangement of these boundaries.
scope: spicule-forming organisms, especially sponges and radiolaria
measurable_quantities: location of spicule deposition relative to cell and vacuole boundaries
correspondence of spicule geometry with boundary geometry
candidate_data: Electron microscopy of sponge sclerocytes and radiolarian skeletogenesis (e.g. EMPIAR, Cell Image Library) and radiolarian image collections.

label: Membranes and cysts form only after protoplasm rounds up with positive surface tension
claim: Because adsorption requires a surface tension greater than zero, films or threads of creeping protoplasm do not form an encysting membrane, and an organism forms its cyst or cell-wall only when its protoplasm has developed a positive surface tension and gathered into a roughly spherical body.
quote: It is for this reason that films or threads of creeping protoplasm shew little tendency, or none, to cover themselves with an encysting membrane; and that it is only when, in an altered phase, the protoplasm has developed a positive surface tension, and has accordingly gathered itself up into a more or less spherical body, that the tendency to form a membrane is manifested
scope: amoeboid and plasmodial protists that encyst
measurable_quantities: timing of cyst-wall deposition relative to cell rounding
candidate_data: Time-lapse encystment studies of Acanthamoeba, Entamoeba or Physarum; Image Data Resource time-lapse datasets.

label: Winter encystment and winter-egg shells relate to temperature effects on adsorption
claim: Since a rise of temperature reduces adsorbability (and surface tension), lower temperature favours adsorption and membrane formation, which probably accounts for the encystment of unicellular organisms at the approach of winter and the strong shells or capsules of winter eggs.
quote: We may in all probability ascribe to this fact and to its converse, or at least associate with it, such phenomena as the encystment of unicellular organisms at the approach of winter, or the frequent formation of strong shells or membranous capsules in “winter-eggs.”
scope: encysting protists and invertebrates producing winter or resting eggs
measurable_quantities: egg shell thickness versus temperature or season
candidate_data: Published Daphnia ephippia and rotifer resting-egg induction experiments and protist encystment-temperature studies (e.g. Dryad datasets).

label: Chondriosomes and similar fibrils are surface-tension clumps drawn along the cell axis
claim: The mitochondria, chondriosomes and similar granules and fibrils of cells are not special entities with specific functions but clumps of heterogeneous cell contents gathered by surface tension and drawn out along the cell axis by osmotic currents arising from surface energy and adsorption, revealing a field of force and dynamical polarity in the cell.
quote: while, from the physical point of view we are tempted to see but little mystery in the whole phenomenon, and to ascribe it, in all probability and in general terms, to the gathering or “clumping” together, under surface tension, of various constituents of the heterogeneous cell-content, and to the drawing out of these little clumps along the axis of the cell towards one or other of its extremities
scope: fibrillar and granular cytoplasmic structures of epithelial, gland, nerve and germ cells
measurable_quantities: orientation of mitochondria relative to cell axis
dependence of their arrangement on cytoplasmic flows
candidate_data: Mitochondrial imaging in the Allen Cell Explorer and Human Protein Atlas subcellular atlas, with studies of cytoplasmic streaming.

label: Potassium salts concentrate where cell-surface tension is weak
claim: Potassium salts, like inorganic substances generally, raise surface tension and therefore concentrate at those parts of a cell surface where the tension is weak, so their localised accumulation (shown by Macallum's cobalt-nitrite method) indicates inequalities of surface tension.
quote: and we may safely take it that our potassium salts, like inorganic substances in general, tend to _raise_ the surface tension, and will therefore be found concentrating at a portion of the surface whose tension is weak
scope: plant and animal cells, solitary and in tissues
measurable_quantities: local potassium concentration at cell surfaces
candidate_data: Potassium-sensitive fluorescent indicator imaging and X-ray microanalysis studies of cells; no dedicated database known.

label: Conjugation outgrowths and root-hairs arise at sites of potassium concentration
claim: The bulges that begin conjugation in algae such as Pleurocarpus and Mesocarpus, and the root-hair outgrowth of Equisetum spores, arise where surface tension is weakened, and these sites coincide with heavy concentrations of potassium salts, which disperse when the cell becomes symmetrical again.
quote: This bulge is, in the first place, a sign of weakened surface tension on one side of the cell, which as a whole had hitherto been a symmetrical cylinder; in the second place, we see that the bulging area corresponds to the position of a great concentration of the potassic salt
scope: conjugating zygnematacean algae, germinating Equisetum spores and other cells forming local outgrowths
measurable_quantities: potassium concentration at outgrowth sites versus elsewhere
timing of potassium accumulation relative to bulging
candidate_data: Ion imaging studies of tip growth in root hairs and pollen tubes and of algal conjugation; no dedicated database known.

label: Potassium accumulates at the bases of cilia and flagella
claim: Ciliate and flagellate cells show a characteristic accumulation of potassium at and near the base of their cilia, which accounts (through weakened surface tension) for the small protuberance where a flagellum arises and the ridge at the base of a row of cilia.
quote: In the case of ciliate or flagellate cells, there is to be found a characteristic accumulation of potassium at and near the base of the cilia.
scope: ciliated and flagellated cells, e.g. Vorticella and monads
measurable_quantities: local surface protrusion at flagellar base
candidate_data: Ion imaging and elemental microanalysis of ciliated cells; ciliary proteomics resources such as CiliaCarta do not directly address ions.

label: Unicellular forms and their asymmetries follow surface molecular forces
claim: In unicellular organisms not only the general configuration but also the departures from symmetry can be correlated with molecular forces, especially local variations of surface tension, acting in their fluid or semifluid surfaces.
quote: we have arrived at the conclusion, as regards unicellular organisms, that not only their general configuration but also _their departures from symmetry_ may be correlated with the molecular forces manifested in their fluid or semi-fluid surfaces.
scope: unicellular organisms
measurable_quantities: spatial distribution of surface tension or cortical tension
candidate_data: Combined cell-shape imaging (Allen Cell Explorer, Image Data Resource) and cortical tension mapping studies.
